content: Postnatal home visits provide a valuable opportunity to evaluate the home environment. Various approaches to postnatal home visits have been implemented, primarily to ensure early postnatal care for mothers and newborns. These visits may occur after discharge from healthcare facilities, as a replacement or supplement to outpatient postnatal care, or as part of community-based care packages, particularly in rural areas. For instance, postnatal home visits are often scheduled within 5 to 9 days following cesarean births. There has been a consistent reduction in the duration of time that mothers and newborns spend in healthcare facilities after delivery. Shorter postnatal stays have been encouraged in some settings to reduce medicalization of the immediate postnatal period and to promote maternal-infant bonding and satisfaction. However, concerns have been raised that early discharge from healthcare facilities may delay the identification and management of maternal and newborn complications. It may also leave insufficient time to prepare women and families for the transition to home, especially in cases where community support is inadequate or absent. Observational studies have examined the relationship between the length of postnatal hospital stays for healthy mothers and newborns and associated outcomes. These studies have yielded mixed results regarding neonatal mortality, infant readmissions, and breastfeeding initiation and duration. Decision-making about discharge readiness is complex and must consider not only the physical health of the mother and newborn but also the mother’s birth experience, her learning needs, and the family’s ability to support the care of the mother and newborn. Discharge readiness is closely linked to the quality of discharge preparation, underscoring the critical role of healthcare workers in this process. Involving men in postnatal care and maternal-newborn health is promoted as an effective strategy to improve health outcomes. Men’s practical, emotional, and financial support can help women and newborns access essential health services and provide support for the mother’s self-care. This involvement also enhances family care practices. Evidence suggests that engaging men in their roles as partners and fathers can serve as an entry point for promoting gender-transformative changes within households and couple relationships. Since the publication of the 2015 WHO recommendations on involving men in maternal and newborn health, systematic reviews and evidence mapping exercises have expanded the evidence base. Women generally desire a positive postnatal experience that allows them to adapt to their new identity, develop confidence and competence as mothers, and adjust to changes in their intimate and family relationships. They also value support in navigating physical and emotional challenges and achieving personal growth as they adapt to their new normal. The WHO recommends a minimum of four postnatal care contacts. For facility-based births, healthy mothers and newborns should receive postnatal care in the facility for at least 24 hours after delivery. For home births, the first postnatal contact should occur as early as possible within 24 hours of birth. At least three additional postnatal contacts are recommended for healthy mothers and newborns: between 48 and 72 hours, between 7 and 14 days, and during the sixth week after birth. The number, timing, and content of postnatal care contacts should be tailored to the health outcomes and needs of the mother and newborn, as well as the home environment and other factors influencing care. Evidence from systematic reviews indicates that most maternal and neonatal deaths occur within the first three days after birth, particularly on the day of birth, with another peak during the second week postpartum. Transition to well-woman and well-infant care typically occurs around six weeks postpartum, including referrals for infant immunizations and family planning services. Structured schedules for postnatal home visits have been evaluated in randomized controlled trials (RCTs). These trials compared different schedules, such as four home visits (on days 3, 7, 28, and 42) versus one home visit at approximately 42 days postpartum. The evidence on maternal and neonatal outcomes, such as morbidity, mortality, and breastfeeding, remains uncertain due to very low-certainty evidence. Similarly, trials comparing two postnatal visits (on days 3–5 and 10–14) versus one outpatient visit (on days 10–14) have not provided conclusive evidence on maternal or newborn outcomes. Women often experience low mood, loneliness, anxiety, and fatigue during the postnatal period. They value the advice, reassurance, and support provided by healthcare workers and family members. Some women may struggle with trauma from labor and birth, difficulties with breastfeeding, or challenges in embracing their maternal identity. Regular engagement with healthcare workers is crucial to address these concerns. Women also tend to prioritize their baby’s needs during the postnatal period, valuing clinical and developmental outcomes for their infant. Economic evaluations of more frequent versus less frequent postnatal care contacts are limited. However, schedules involving more contacts may increase service costs and require additional staff time and resources. Continuity of care is highly valued by women and healthcare workers, as it fosters supportive, caring, and trusting relationships and improves the overall experience of care. In settings with well-functioning midwifery programs, midwife-led continuity-of-care models can ensure consistent postnatal care. Routine postnatal care contacts may also be complemented by phone-based follow-ups or digital communication tools.
